project.name: Unifolio code
project.description: Unifolio is a mutual fund portfolio tracking and wealth-management platform for the Indian market (MF-only MVP): CAS import, onboarding, a main holdings dashboard, and an analytics dashboard, built with a FastAPI/Python backend and a Vite/React frontend. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: PRODUCT.md lays out what Unifolio actually is: a mutual-fund portfolio tracking and wealth-management platform for the Indian market, positioned as a free-core, genuinely superior alternative to Mprofit. It defines the target users, the operating constraints, and the accessibility and brand commitments that shape every feature decision that follows. The repo's own README is a placeholder, so this brief is the real starting point for understanding why the codebase is organized the way it is.

tour.title: Backend Entry Point
tour.description: main.py is where the FastAPI application comes to life: it constructs the app, wires up CORS, mounts every feature router (auth, CAS imports, dashboard, analytics), manages the shared Playwright browser lifecycle used for CAS PDF parsing, and exposes a health-check endpoint. As the highest-scoring code entry point and the root of the backend's dependency graph, this is the natural place to start reading the backend half of the monorepo.

tour.title: Backend API Routers
tour.description: These four routers are what main.py mounts, and together they define the entire HTTP surface of the product: auth.py handles OTP/OAuth login and session management, imports.py drives CAS statement upload and history, dashboard.py exposes holdings/allocation/SIP data, and analytics.py serves fund scores and benchmark comparisons. Each router is intentionally thin, delegating real work to a matching service module — a pattern you'll see repeated as the tour goes deeper.

tour.title: Core Domain Models
tour.description: These SQLAlchemy models are the most depended-upon files in the entire backend, which makes sense: they define the vocabulary every router and service in Step 3 relies on. enums.py centralizes every domain enum (investor type, import status, transaction type), user.py defines the User/HouseholdMember identity model, folio.py and transaction.py capture the folio/transaction-level financial data, and reference.py holds the fund master data (schemes, NAV history, expense ratios, computed fund scores) that the analytics engine consumes later.
tour.languageLesson: SQLAlchemy models double as the single source of truth for both the Python ORM layer and (via Alembic) the actual database schema — the enum_column helper in enums.py keeps enum-backed columns declared consistently across every model.

tour.title: Database Schema Reference
tour.description: This PRD documents the relational schema underpinning the models from Step 4 — an ER diagram plus entity definitions for users, household members, imports, schemes, folios, transactions, NAV/TER/AAUM reference data, fund scores, auth identities, OTP requests, and sessions. It's the design document the ORM models were built to satisfy, so reading it alongside Step 4 clarifies why the tables are shaped the way they are, including data-classification and indexing notes that don't live in the code itself.
tour.languageLesson: Keeping a schema PRD separate from the ORM models lets the design intent (why a relationship or index exists) survive independently of implementation details that change as migrations evolve.

tour.title: CAS Import Pipeline
tour.description: Building on the folio and transaction models from Step 4, this service layer implements the product's hardest problem: parsing password-protected CAS (Consolidated Account Statement) PDFs and reconciling their transactions/folios/schemes against what's already in the database. service.py handles the in-memory parsing workflow, while lifecycle_service.py orchestrates the end-to-end import lifecycle across cross-account data. This is the feature that lets a user go from a raw statement PDF to a populated portfolio.

tour.title: Analytics & Fund Scoring Engine
tour.description: This is the core fund-rating engine behind the Analytics dashboard. scorer.py computes a risk-adjusted, TER-aware score per scheme and rolls it up into a holdings-weighted portfolio score; benchmark.py computes portfolio- and fund-level XIRR against Nifty benchmark indices; recompute.py orchestrates the whole household recompute pipeline with generation-based optimistic-concurrency locking so only one recompute runs per user at a time. Together they turn the raw transaction data from Step 6 into the scores and comparisons users see.
tour.languageLesson: The generation-based claim/release locking in recompute.py is a concurrency pattern worth noting: instead of a database-level lock, a monotonically increasing generation counter lets the service detect and discard stale recompute attempts.

tour.title: Frontend Entry Point
tour.description: Switching to the other half of the stack: main.tsx mounts the root React app (or a dedicated print-analytics view, depending on route) into the DOM. App.tsx is what it mounts — the root component that picks a mobile or desktop shell, wires up the AuthProvider, and routes signed-in users to onboarding, the main dashboard, or a pending-deletion screen. This is the frontend's mirror of Step 2's backend entry point.

tour.title: Auth & Onboarding Flow
tour.description: AuthContext.tsx holds the frontend's session state and exposes login/logout/contact-change/account-deletion operations that talk to the auth.py router from Step 3. AuthEntryFlow.tsx implements the phone/email OTP sign-up and sign-in screens, and OnboardingFlow.tsx orchestrates the multi-step post-signup questionnaire (investing experience, household setup, CAS import, family import) that a new user walks through before reaching the dashboard.
tour.languageLesson: AuthContext.tsx uses React Context to make session state available throughout the component tree without prop-drilling — App.tsx (Step 8) wraps its routes in this provider once, near the root.

tour.title: Dashboard Data Layer
tour.description: DashboardView.tsx is the main holdings dashboard: it fetches aggregate and per-member holdings, allocation, SIPs, cash-flow, and XIRR data, then renders summary cards, allocation tabs, and drill-down modals — consuming the dashboard.py endpoints from Step 3. import/api.ts and analytics/types.ts round out the feature-level API clients and shared types that keep the CAS import and analytics data flowing between the backend services from Steps 6-7 and the UI.

tour.title: Containerization
tour.description: The backend Dockerfile packages the FastAPI app (plus Playwright/Chromium, needed for CAS PDF parsing from Step 6) into a single-stage production image based on python:3.12-slim. docker-compose.yml is the local development counterpart, running a Postgres 16 container as the backend's test database, matching the production database engine target described in the Migration-Plan PRD.
tour.languageLesson: This Dockerfile uses a single build stage rather than a multi-stage build, which is a reasonable tradeoff when the runtime dependency (Playwright/Chromium) is also needed at build time and image size is a secondary concern to build simplicity.

tour.title: CI/CD & Cloud Infrastructure
tour.description: ci.yml is the GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every push and PR, executing backend pytest and frontend Vitest suites before anything ships. The Terraform modules take over from there: infra/modules/backend/main.tf provisions the staging backend on ECS Fargate (cluster, task definitions, an ALB with HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect), while infra/envs/staging/main.tf is the root module that wires networking, database, ECR, backend, scheduler, and DNS together into the full AWS stack the containerized app from Step 11 actually runs on.
tour.languageLesson: Terraform resources declare desired infrastructure state rather than imperative steps — the root module in infra/envs/staging/main.tf composes smaller reusable modules (like infra/modules/backend) rather than declaring every resource inline.
